title: Import: dedupe keys, near-duplicate decisions, date and decimal detection, MoneyWiz layouts
notes: Date format and decimal style are detected ONCE per file over the whole column — never per row, so one file can never mix interpretations.
The dedupe key is a readable string, not a digest: accountId|date|amountMinor|normalised-payee-or-description (D10).
An EXACT duplicate (identical key) is auto-skipped and counted. A NEAR duplicate (same account, same amount, ±1 day, similar payee) is always a human decision.
An unparseable date or amount makes the ROW an error; it is never rounded, shifted or guessed into shape.
MoneyWiz Report detection MUST be tested before flat MoneyWiz detection: a Report file passes both.

In the Report layout the account header row carries the account CURRENCY in its “Account” column, and openingBalance = statedBalance − Σ(rows) — refused (null) when any of that account’s rows will not import.
Ops named import.reportOpeningBalances / import.reportCategoryPaths / import.reportRows are PROJECTIONS of parseMoneyWizReportCsv’s single result, not separate functions.
Warning text is English prose for a human; a re-implementation is bound by when a warning is raised, not by its wording.

cases.describes: case folded, punctuation dropped, whitespace collapsed and trimmed
runs of whitespace collapse to one space
letters keep their accents — only punctuation and symbols go
a reference code loses its symbols but keeps its digits
a purely numeric reference keeps every digit
whitespace normalises to the empty key
the dedupe key is the readable string accountId|date|amountMinor|normalised-payee (D10) — not a digest, so a mismatch can be read by a human
the sign is part of the key: a £45.67 refund is not a duplicate of a £45.67 charge
with no payee the description takes its place, so a re-import matches a manual entry made the same way
the textbook kitten/sitting distance of three edits
identical strings are distance 0
an empty string is its length away
one deleted character is one edit away
a transposition costs TWO edits — this is Levenshtein, not Damerau-Levenshtein
normalised equality — case never distinguishes payees
the shorter contained in the longer (minimum 3 characters)
containment needs at least 3 characters, and “ab” is six edits from “ab store” — well outside the 25% threshold, so these are different payees
within max(1, 25% of the longer length) edits
plainly different payees do not match
the same payee written with and without symbols
two blank payees are “the same” — the date and amount then carry the decision
a blank payee never matches a named one
an identical dedupe key is an EXACT duplicate — auto-skipped, with a count shown
the key is normalised, so “TESCO!” on the same day for the same amount is still exact
same account, same amount, one day apart, similar payee ⇒ NEAR duplicate: flagged for a human, never dropped and never doubled
with both a same-day and a next-day candidate, the SAME-DAY one is reported
two days apart is not a near duplicate — the window is ±1 day
a penny different is a different transaction
a refund of the same magnitude is not a duplicate of the charge
the same purchase on a DIFFERENT account is not a duplicate — acc2 holds an identical row and is ignored
same day and same amount but an unrelated payee is a genuine second transaction
a first component above 12 settles it as dd/mm
a middle component above 12 settles it as mm/dd
ambiguous ⇒ en-GB dd/mm (D20) — the 5th of June
the caller can override, because an all-ambiguous US export is otherwise unfixable — the 6th of May
a 4-digit lead is ISO order
a 4-digit lead means ISO order even with slash separators
dot separators, as continental exports write them
dash separators in day-month-year order
a 2-digit year is expanded, not treated as year 26
the 2-digit-year pivot: 49 ⇒ 2049
and the other side of the pivot: 50 becomes 1950
a trailing time component is dropped — the calendar date is what is stored
a spelled-out short month between day and year
with the month spelled out
a US-style month-name-first date with a comma
29 February exists in a leap year
and does not in a common year — the row is refused, not shifted to 1 March
an impossible date is refused
a 3-digit year is refused rather than guessed at
text that is not a date at all yields no date
an empty cell has no date, and the row becomes an error
ONE value with a first component above 12 settles the WHOLE column as dd/mm
and one with a middle component above 12 settles it as mm/dd
a 4-digit lead ANYWHERE in the column wins outright
a column that stays ambiguous falls back to en-GB dd/mm
an empty column falls back too
unreadable values are ignored by the vote rather than derailing it
dots group and the comma is the decimal
commas group and the dot is the decimal
“1,234” with THREE trailing digits is grouping, not a decimal — so the file is dot style
and “1.234” with three trailing digits in a 2-decimal currency is dot-grouping ⇒ comma style
the SAME string in a 3-decimal currency is a plain amount ⇒ dot style — the currency decides
in a 0-decimal currency (JPY) no separator can be a decimal point, so every one is grouping
a column with no separators at all defaults to dot
when both separators appear in one value, the LAST one is the decimal
a decimal comma with no grouping separator
dot grouping with a decimal comma
accounting parentheses are negative
symbol and grouping stripped
auto: three trailing digits after a lone comma is GROUPING — £1,234.00, not £12.34
auto: two trailing digits after a lone comma is a DECIMAL — £45.67
a 0-decimal currency takes the digits as they stand
and refuses a fraction rather than rounding it away
a 3-decimal currency keeps all three
more precision than the currency has is refused, so the row surfaces as an error
words in an amount column yield no amount, so the row errors
an empty amount cell is refused rather than read as zero
a sign inside the number is refused
a negative zero amount is plain zero
a trailing ISO code is stripped

THE PRECEDENCE TRAP: a Report file answers YES to the flat MoneyWiz test as well, so the Report test MUST be asked first — read with the flat parser, every account header row becomes a dateless transaction and no opening balance is ever derived
a flat MoneyWiz export has neither a Name nor a Current balance column, so the Report test cannot steal it
an ordinary bank CSV is neither, and goes to the mapped generic importer

the reason this parser exists: opening balance = the file’s stated Current balance MINUS the sum of that account’s rows, which is order-independent and so immune to the export’s unreliable running-balance column

cases.describes: “/” is a level separator ONLY when the column contains no “►” or “>” anywhere: “Home/Repairs” alone becomes two levels…
